eligibility.evidence: Sect. 2.1-2.3, 3.2, Table 1-2: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct makes a binary choice (token 2 vs 3) under five valence framings; the authors call it a framing effect and compare the shift with human framing studies (Tversky & Kahneman 1981, ref. 11). Borderline because the task comes from an AI-interpretability paper (Bianco & Shiller 2026), not a human experiment.

A.title: Behavioral Evidence of Valence-Driven Choice Modulation in Qwen2.5-7B: A Bianco-Shiller (2026) Replication Study
A.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

paradigms.name: Valence-framed binary token choice (2 vs 3) with five framing conditions
paradigms.source_paper: Bianco & Shiller (2026), arXiv:2602.19159; Tversky & Kahneman (1981) cited for human framing magnitude

effects.es_metric: difference in proportion choosing 2, low-pressure minus high-pressure (delta F_H)
effects.label: NO-HUMAN-REFERENCE
effects.location: Abstract; Sect. 3.1-3.2; Table 2 (stochastic, temperature 0.8, n=30-40 per condition); chi-square p<0.001 stated in abstract

E.headline: High-threat framing reverses Qwen2.5-7B's default choice (delta 0.63), replicating the Gemma-2-9B behavioural finding on a second model family.

G.notes: Single model, self-funded, no affiliation; prompts only abbreviated; no code link; n given as 30-40 per condition. Human framing benchmark (10-30 percent shifts) is a loose citation, not data. Task has no intrinsic option value, so a framing effect is arguable; referee would question E2 provenance.
